items.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
items.summary: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
items.content:
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.

In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.

For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.

Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.

Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.

Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.

But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."

"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."

There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"

Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".

"If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.

Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.

But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.

With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.

Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.

Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.

All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.

And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.

And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.

I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".

Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.

Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.

"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.

Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.

items.title: Horible public key tricks
items.summary: Article URL: https://maurycyz.com/projects/badcert/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50434264 Points: 177 # Comments: 58
items.content:
So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.

... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"

There is prior art of protest SSL implementations , but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.

The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it.

# openssl s_client -connect maurycyz.com : 443 /dev/null \ | sed -n /BEGIN/,/END/p | grep -zE '////.?*////' --color= yes -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIFAjCCA+qgAwIBAgISBkOkuuyaN1ypD3PAPrLMyT7tMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBCwUA MDMxCzAJBgNVBAYTAlVTMRYwFAYDVQQKEw1MZXQncyBFbmNyeXB0MQwwCgYDVQQD EwNZUjIwHhcNMjYxMTA5MTcyOTQ2WhcNMjcwMjA3MTcyOTQ1WjAXMRUwEwYDVQQD EwxtYXVyeWN5ei5jb20wggEiMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4IBDwAwggEKAoIBAQCg JyPf37Sj6PvU06m5 ////You+dont+actually+have+to+pick+random+privat e+keys//No+one+checks+these+things//A+certificate+authority+got+ away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year///// DSfCAfXcsJfBpnHekS0qnf5YLl c54VuUNRVINcDkEwJDwyB96+xE/uXhtiGdk8ty1PF6jciLEYCJBHcmqOa5pOyV8m 63yR3NE6hCQlaSLQQDo96Sb0/10aC5LqE7KwEskrP/qeCzT7vDN7fh+dXOGs+VMw eJvTAb0xHJpxhSK05i7DAgMBAAGjggIqMIICJjAOBgNVHQ8BAf8EBAMCBaAwEwYD VR0lBAwwCgYIKwYBBQUHAwEwDAYDVR0TAQH/BAIwADAdBgNVHQ4EFgQUBKBfDbwf dCnKeU83pMTWyFrJBwAwHwYDVR0jBBgwFoAUQBUtJnntMiCe35pyHdYyH4EMgQww MwYIKwYBBQUHAQEEJzAlMCMGCCsGAQUFBzAChhdodHRwOi8veXIyLmkubGVuY3Iu b3JnLzAnBgNVHREEIDAegg4qLm1hdXJ5Y3l6LmNvbYIMbWF1cnljeXouY29tMBMG A1UdIAQMMAowCAYGZ4EMAQIBMC8GA1UdHwQoMCYwJKAioCCGHmh0dHA6Ly95cjIu Yy5sZW5jci5vcmcvMTEwLmNybDCCAQsGCisGAQQB1nkCBAIEgfwEgfkA9wB1AExj 3JjlnB2riPYeij3ero+rRKM3e1+blMP7oZz8wb4mAAABocGRbw4AAAQDAEYwRAIg HShWaEI2nVJEizSI6sJ/jnLaABZ3aTKoUL3pLo1uOgsCIEn+XiT2WHhm9LGN6kug O9R7Z4q0HiFA4RZ7tIMJQH5XAH4AjspHC6zeavOiBrCkeoS3Rv4fxr+VPiXmm07k AkjzxugAAAGhwZFyfQAIAAAFAEE0hdwEAwBHMEUCIDSms4Vf0llcvcldJd2Ool8i AiUQQlS0Zzbej+7Y1aR7AiEA79Ll+t6inu1PkUIgzNTXkE0S20VHYEYel5fkdKSA VTQwDQYJKoZIhvcNAQELBQADggEBAFi3A4fcjj4UKa9MFz1a8DWc+Jya2gJng13m 2UFdWCaqsN7FJWQEjRiJ0npynmDnA3VMyjswUMHAMx4d8G3lHNPfZWGsCgpjVa/d IEoeZ6gTYjFa/Ovb64m4CcuQkm0GxcyAqMPs348e6Px32iU1R6MnV4UEUosnSPeK 4ocuI3SoR9LHxX/yHOKcYTKLpIMwMdaAmWt0N7l59GOb8o+dz3R7cxtVV/lrZReZ /YPEAYRiNi7f+jNI1JCp0i8wXUb9NN7WlbmcFDecDG/++cRpAkoIk4m/LJindsuu kErrVZ4yLqB0Hvm+uNvWxr9y/qKFTYw9POx1oaZJO/SwXZdDBeY= -----END CERTIFICATE-----

First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent.

The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent:

# Encryption requires knowing e (public) cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n

The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q.

# Decryption requires knowing d (pivate) = cyphertext^d mod n = plaintext^e^d mod n = plaintext^(e*d) mod n = plaintext^1 mod n = plaintext

Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.

The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.

My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.

The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product:

58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176 (incrementing until the next prime...) 58174124 * 9184918 43 = 5343245836 7670532

As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner.

From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key:

# Single domain openssl req -new -key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request # Wildcard cat > config [ req ] req_extensions = req_ext [ req_ext ] subjectAltName = @alt_names [ alt_names ] DNS.1 = *.example.com DNS.2 = example.com EOF openssl req -new -key priv.pem -config config -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request ... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts.

The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.

Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) avalable charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice.

As for security , this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. However, it should still be secure: nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression. If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key.

A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security... although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys.

The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also be a problem. Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values

However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised.

items.title: What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
items.summary: The billionaire tech executive finds himself mired in a personal and national security scandal.
items.content:
One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report.

On Sunday, Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company.

President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair .

The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC.

Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.

However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.

"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China."

The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf.

Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times.

Nvidia shares slide as US tech giant investigates CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers.

Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero.

Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China .

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff.

He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.

Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.

"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".

Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates .

Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch.

"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them," Witt told the BBC.

Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft, now use Nvidia chips.

Currently worth $4.5tn (£3.4tn), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies ever.

For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".

Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake.

There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy.

His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles.

Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners.

They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.

In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.

Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

Witt told the BBC that Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

"È emerso che il vaudeville tragicomico sulla minaccia degli 'hacker filorussi' è stato interamente messo in scena dalla componente più aggressiva e militarista dell'élite politica italiana, al solo scopo di 'vendere' l'ennesimo pacchetto di aiuti militari e finanziari al corrotto regime di Zelensky". Ad affermarlo è l'ambasciata della Russia in Italia in un post su Telegram dopo che ieri aveva già schernito le difese cyber dell'Italia offrendo sarcasticamente l'aiuto dei propri specialisti. Forse, sottolinea l'Ambasciata russa, "neppure in un Paese dalle ricche tradizioni teatrali, come l'Italia, era mai capitato che esponenti politici s'immedesimassero così a fondo nel ruolo di vittime innocenti». È stato qui sfoderato l'intero repertorio teatrale: la mimica, la gestualità, l'ostentazione emotiva di paura e impotenza di fronte ai malvagi, la sconfinata bontà e il risentimento di un padre di famiglia senza colpa alcuna, l'esibizione di animali domestici per accattivarsi le simpatie del pubblico". L'esito, conclude, "è stato poco convincente e, a tratti, decisamente falso. La sola cosa tragica qui è che Roma, invece di contribuire alla causa della pace - come la esortano con forza le menti più illuminate d'Italia e l'opinione pubblica - si lasci trascinare dal partito della guerra, allontanandosi sempre più dalla propria tradizione diplomatica e dagli aneliti alla pace della popolazione. Tanto più doloroso sarà risvegliarsi dalle illusioni imposte all'Italia dagli aguzzini di Kiev e dagli ipnotizzatori di Bruxelles"

Dalla Danimarca 720 milioni di euro per sostegno militare a Kiev

La Danimarca donerà 720 milioni di dollari in sostegno militare all'Ucraina. Lo ha annunciato il ministro degli Esteri danese, Esteri Lars Lkke mentre il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky è atteso a Copenaghen per un incontro con i leader dei Paesi nordici. Il ministrod anese ha dato l'annuncio ai giornalisti al termine di una riunione con la commissione per la politica estera del Parlamento danese, aggiungendo che la Danimarca donerà inoltre 150 milioni di corone al settore energetico ucraino.

Zelensky: “Se cessa il loro aiuto, conseguenze pericolose per gli europei”

"Un atteggiamento scettico nei confronti dell'aiuto all'Ucraina non è vantaggioso per nessun paese europeo, perché in realtà si tratta di affrontare la Russia. La Russia si oppone alle regole e ai valori europei. Da un punto di vista pragmatico, avere un'Ucraina forte è importante, anzi, necessario. Se l'aiuto europeo dovesse cessare, le conseguenze potrebbero essere solo pericolose o estremamente pericolose". Lo afferma il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky. Per il leader ucraino, nello scenario più blando "la Russia continuerebbe i suoi attacchi ibridi, come ha già fatto più volte in Moldavia, Romania, Bulgaria, e persino in Germania e nei paesi del Nord Europa, come Finlandia e Danimarca. Inizieranno a farlo su larga scala". Nello scenario peggiore "la Russia avanzerebbe ulteriormente in Europa. Putin vuole riportare indietro e tornare all'Urss. Cosa significa? Avere influenza sui paesi dell'ex Urss, almeno sui paesi baltici e sulla Moldavia. Ciò significa anche che si tratta di paesi che fanno parte della Nato, e questo implicherebbe che la Nato dovrà reagire. Sarà coinvolta tutta l'Europa e gli Stati Uniti".

Il segretario di Stato americano Marco Rubio ha adottato un tono cauto sui colloqui di Abu Dhabi, affermando che il processo per porre fine alla guerra è ancora "lungo da percorrere". "Continueremo a provarci. Ed è quello che abbiamo cercato di fare fin dall'inizio: essere creativi e trovare modi per contribuire a porre fine a questo conflitto e a questa guerra", ha detto Rubio, secondo quanto riporta Al Jazeera

Witkoff: Nato forte resta fondamentale per difesa collettiva

"I partecipanti hanno ribadito il loro impegno comune a favore di una solida architettura e di accordi di sicurezza europei nel dopoguerra, affermando chiaramente che una Nato forte rimarrà fondamentale per la difesa collettiva euro-atlantica". È quanto fa sapere l'inviato speciale Usa Steve Witkoff in un post sul social X dopo l'incontro con i rappresentanti dell'Ucraina, dell'Ue, tra cui l'Italia, e del Regno Unito prima dell'inizio dei colloqui trilaterali ad Abu Dhabi, negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, tra Stati Uniti, Ucraina e Russia

Nessun rappresentante dell'Unione europea sta partecipando ai negoziati sull'Ucraina ad Abu Dhabi. Lo ha ribadito il viceministro russo degli Esteri Aleksandr Grusko. "Non sono parte del processo", ha affermato Grusko martedì, parlando con i giornalisti. "E' sottinteso che sia gli americani che gli ucraini si consulteranno con loro", ha aggiunto. "Finora, gli europei hanno agito come elementi di disturbo del processo e non vedo alcun fattore che possa modificare questo loro atteggiamento", ha concluso

Witkoff dopo incontro con Ue e Kiev: qualsiasi accordo rispetti integrità ucraina

"I partecipanti hanno sottolineato che qualsiasi accordo futuro dovrà rispettare la sovranità, l'integrità territoriale e l'autonomia decisionale, oltre a fornire garanzie di sicurezza credibili per l'Ucraina". Lo afferma l'inviato speciale americano Steve Witkoff su X dopo l'incontro tra Usa, europei e ucraini a margine degli incontri a Abu Dhabi. "In vista delle imminenti discussioni trilaterali con la Russia, - afferma Witkoff - i rappresentanti degli Stati Uniti, dell'Ucraina e dei partner europei si sono incontrati per proseguire il loro stretto coordinamento sugli sforzi volti a porre fine alla guerra in Ucraina e a creare le condizioni per una pace duratura, compreso il sostegno a solide garanzie di sicurezza nell'ambito di qualsiasi accordo. Le discussioni si sono svolte in uno spirito di collaborazione tra gli Stati Uniti, l'Ucraina e i partner europei, riflettendo i loro obiettivi condivisi, le consultazioni in corso e l'impegno a favore della sicurezza euro-atlantica". L'obiettivo, aggiunge l'inviato Usa, "condiviso è quello di sviluppare un quadro di sicurezza pratico e sinergico che rafforzi la sicurezza a lungo termine dell'Ucraina e crei la fiducia necessaria per raggiungere una soluzione negoziata"

Gli Stati Uniti "non si sono mai opposti" a colloqui diretti tra Europa e Russia, "erano i russi a non volerlo". Lo ha dichiarato il segretario di Stato Usa, Marco Rubio, in un incontro con la stampa americana a margine del G7 a Parigi, sottolineando che ad Abu Dhabi "sono presenti" rappresentanti europei. "La strada da fare è ancora lunga. Comunque, è un bene che stiano dialogando, è positivo che i colloqui trilaterali siano ripresi. E' sempre meglio che non avere alcun dialogo", ha aggiunto Rubio

L'inviato di Donald Trump, Jared Kushner, ha auspicato un "nuovo" quadro di sicurezza per l'Ucraina e la Russia, ma anche per l'Europa, in apertura dei colloqui ad Abu Dhabi tra Kiev e Mosca, sotto la mediazione statunitense. "L'auspicio oggi non è soltanto quello di discutere di questioni bilaterali e di come porre fine alla guerra, ma anche di stabilire come instaurare solide relazioni in ambito di sicurezza tra Ucraina, Russia ed Europa, affinchè non solo si metta fine a questo conflitto, ma si definisca anche un nuovo quadro di riferimento", ha dichiarato.

Capo delegazione russa: “Speriamo che i colloqui avvicinino alla pace”

Vladimir Medinsky, capo della delegazione russa ad Abu Dhabi e consigliere presidenziale, ha espresso la speranza che i colloqui trilaterali con Usa e Ucraina consentano di "compiere progressi verso la pace". "Ci auguriamo che l'incontro odierno, con la sua composizione rappresentativa, la nostra delegazione ora più ampia e ancora più professionale, ci permetta di avanzare verso la pace nell'interesse dei popoli di Russia e Ucraina", ha dichiarato in apertura dei colloqui Medinsky, citato da Tass.

L'Italia ha partecipato questa mattina ad Abu Dhabi, con il consigliere per la sicurezza nazionale, Fabrizio Saggio, alla riunione di coordinamento con gli inviati statunitensi Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, che ha preceduto l'avvio dei colloqui trilaterali tra Stati Uniti, Ucraina e Russia. Lo riferiscono fonti di Palazzo Chigi. All'incontro hanno partecipato rappresentanti dell'Ucraina, dei Paesi E4 (Germania, Francia, Italia e Regno Unito), della Nato e dell'Ue. Nel corso della riunione, l'Italia - si sottolinea - ha ribadito il pieno sostegno all'Ucraina, alla sua sovranità e integrità territoriale, nonchè agli sforzi degli Stati Uniti per riportare le parti al tavolo negoziale.

items.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
items.summary: The ruling means the case can move forward, possibly with reduced charges in a new trial.
items.content:
A Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children.

The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict.

Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.

The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.

Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice.

Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.

The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight.

In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC.

The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said.

"Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy."

Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.

He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive".

The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March.

Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband says he forgave her so he would not be 'eaten up inside forever'

Lindsay Clancy's trial puts postpartum psychosis in the spotlight

Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.

After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict.

The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.

In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant.

Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.

Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

items.title: The Pope’s Italian basketball player: “The game helped me overcome grief. I dream of the NBA”
items.summary: An interview with Luigi Suigo, Villanova Wildcats player: “I returned to basketball after losing my mother. I dream of the Spurs and study Wembanyama’s game.”
items.content:
As a child, Luigi Suigo grew – and grew fast. He started playing basketball at the age of seven, but by the time he was 11, he had already had to overcome problems with his heels and a far deeper source of pain: the loss of his mother.

He eventually returned to the game, and his journey from Tradate, Italy, took him via Olimpia Milano all the way to the Villanova Wildcats. Based in Pennsylvania, Villanova is the university where Pope Leo XIV graduated with a degree in mathematics in 1977.

In honour of the pontiff, the first NCAA (US college basketball) game between Villanova and Notre Dame was played at Rome's PalaEur, marking an unprecedented transatlantic showcase for American college basketball. Notre Dame won 74–72.

For Suigo, a 221cm (7ft 3in), 127kg (280lb) centre who turns 20 in January, it was his official debut in a Wildcats jersey (He had 16 points and 15 rebounds in the next game, a 95-66 win over Holy Cross).

Last season, the young player from Lombardy enjoyed a solid campaign with Mega Belgrade, the Serbian team that launched Nikola Jokić, a big man who has mastered virtually every aspect of the game with the ball in his hands.

Head coach Kevin Willard has already offered his assessment of Suigo: “He has good fundamentals; he needs to learn how to move in space.” On social media, however, his progress is already being celebrated: he's become SuiGOAT.

“My dad started playing quite late, but he had a great build – he was two metres tall. My mum was 1.80m. I lost her when I was 11, and she had been the one who asked me to stop playing after my heel problems. I went back to basketball to cope with the pain of losing her. We had a little hoop in the garden.”

“The San Antonio Spurs, of course – Victor Wembanyama's team. But also the Boston Celtics.”

People compare you to Victor Wembanyama. How does that feel?

“Wemby is a player I try to learn from and take inspiration from. I haven't had the chance to see him play live yet, and I'd love to do that soon. Maybe I'll get the opportunity at a game somewhere not too far from Villanova.

“I like his style of play and the fact that he can do everything with the ball. He's one of the greatest players ever to play this sport. It's great to be called the Italian Wemby, even though there's an enormous gap between us. I study his game.

“But there's another player I really admire: Latvia's Kristaps Porziņģis, who joined Golden State this season.”

He's certainly nowhere near as much of a media sensation as Wembanyama.

“I think my playing style has some similarities to both of theirs. I hope I can work hard enough to reach the point where people compare me to players of that calibre. But it's too early for that now.” (On November 6, Kristaps Porziņģis announced that he was stepping away from basketball for health reasons.)

“I want to build a physique suited to the NBA, so I can be ready for the draft and have a chance of being picked in a good position.

As the Wildcats, we want to go as far as possible, earn a place in March Madness – the pinnacle of US college basketball – and keep our season going for as long as we can.”

In these first few weeks of training, what are the main differences on the court that you’ve noticed?

“The pace of the game is very different; the way the Americans defend, and even the way the coach asks me to defend, is different from my time in Europe.”

What are the main differences you've noticed on the court during your first few weeks of training?

“The pace of the game is very different. The way Americans defend, and the way the coach asks me to defend, is also different from what I was used to in Europe.”

“The culture behind it: the fans, the people, the lasting bond former students have with that experience, which stays with them long after their university years are over. Even my dad has started following the NCAA season.”

“I'm not particularly religious, but meeting the Pope was something really special. Just like playing in Rome. My teammates and I took a bus through the city centre. It wasn't my first time there, but it was for many of them, and I was struck by the way they looked at the Colosseum. Playing here is cool. It's a really great experience.”

Your first basket for the Italian national team was a three-pointer – not exactly typical for a big man. Luca Banchi, the national team coach who gave you your debut and who famously said when he took the job, “I'm looking for my unicorn” – a centre who can also play away from the basket, like Jokić – was watching you train in Rome. Could you be Italian basketball's unicorn?

“Having Banchi there made me proud. I also met Gigi Datome. Wearing the Italy jersey is something I always have in mind, and I'd put it on whenever I get the chance. Unfortunately, that won't happen very often this season: it's unlikely Villanova will let me come back for international games.

“I've already played four games in the 2027 World Cup qualifiers. The first one, against Iceland, was so-so, but the excitement of playing for Italy got the better of me. I did better in Lithuania, and even better against Great Britain.

items.title: È stato arrestato il fratello dell’ex primo ministro ungherese Viktor Orbán, è indagato per traffico di migranti
items.content:
È stato arrestato in Ungheria Áron Orbán, fratello dell’ex primo ministro ungherese Viktor Orbán. La polizia non ha reso noti i nomi degli arrestati, che in tutto sono quattro, ma in serata un fotografo della testata indipendente ungherese HVG ha fotografato Áron Orbán nell’auto della polizia mentre veniva portato nel carcere di Budapest, dove rimarrà in attesa che un giudice si esprima sulla custodia cautelare.

La polizia ha detto che i quattro arrestati sono accusati di aver sfruttato la vicinanza a persone interne alle istituzioni per far rilasciare visti e permessi di soggiorno ad almeno un centinaio di lavoratori di cittadinanza vietnamita, in cambio di denaro. Sono indagati per traffico di migranti.

Commentando l’arresto del fratello, Viktor Orbán ha sostenuto che si tratti di una «persecuzione politica» contro la sua famiglia, ordita dall’attuale governo di Péter Magyar. «Io sono il vero bersaglio», ha scritto, «mio fratello minore viene semplicemente usato per arrivare a me». Da quando è al governo Magyar ha effettivamente avviato diverse iniziative per smantellare il sistema di potere costruito da Orbán, che in sedici anni aveva favorito abusi e corruzione.

items.title: L’impeachment contro Pete Hegseth è un anticipo dei prossimi due anni
items.summary: La messa sotto accusa del segretario alla Difesa americano difficilmente passerà, ma mostra la debolezza di Trump
items.content:
Thomas Massie, deputato Repubblicano del Kentucky, ha avviato lunedì una procedura di impeachment contro il segretario alla Difesa Pete Hegseth, che potrebbe essere votata alla Camera degli Stati Uniti già mercoledì. Massie accusa Hegseth di aver violato la Costituzione e le leggi federali portando avanti varie guerre illegali.

Tra i capi d’accusa dell’atto di impeachment ci sono: aver portato avanti la guerra in Medio Oriente oltre i limiti concessi dalla legge, perché senza l’autorizzazione del Congresso il presidente potrebbe fare la guerra soltanto per 60 giorni , rinnovabili di altri 30 per il ritiro delle truppe, e invece si è andati molto oltre; aver fatto attacchi militari illegali contro presunti narcotrafficanti; aver catturato illegalmente il presidente venezuelano Nicolás Maduro; aver fatto attacchi senza autorizzazione contro lo Yemen; aver ignorato le leggi che impongono di minimizzare le vittime civili durante una guerra, in questo caso quella contro l’Iran.

Pur essendo un Repubblicano, Massie è un noto critico di Donald Trump e delle guerre approvate dalla sua amministrazione. È anche alla fine del suo mandato: qualche mese fa era stato sconfitto alle primarie del Partito Repubblicano da un candidato sostenuto da Trump, che poi ha vinto il suo seggio alle elezioni di metà mandato e si insedierà al posto di Massie a gennaio. Trump ha definito Massie un «perdente» e ha detto che sosterrà Hegseth nonostante il tentativo di impeachment .

La possibilità che fosse proposto un impeachment contro Hegseth si era presentata molto chiaramente dopo le elezioni di metà mandato della settimana scorsa, vinte in maniera schiacciante dai Democratici. Hegseth è probabilmente il più discusso dei membri dell’amministrazione, e anche quello più debole: la sua gestione della guerra in Medio Oriente è unanimemente considerata fallimentare, e anche molti Repubblicani lo ritengono inadeguato al ruolo.

Negli scorsi giorni si era anche parlato della possibilità – non da escludere in futuro – che Trump stesso chiedesse le sue dimissioni. Secondo vari media americani il vero obiettivo di Massie sarebbe proprio questo: spingere Trump a rimuovere Hegseth.

Per ragioni procedurali il voto alla Camera dovrà essere entro mercoledì. Lo speaker Repubblicano della Camera Mike Johnson ha ancora qualche possibilità di evitarlo: potrebbe chiedere ai deputati di votare per inviare le accuse contro Hegseth a una commissione parlamentare oppure per archiviarle. Se questi tentativi non funzioneranno, la Camera dovrà votare sull’atto di impeachment . Basta una maggioranza semplice per l’approvazione.

In teoria i Repubblicani hanno ancora la maggioranza alla Camera e non dovrebbero aver problemi a bocciare la mozione. Ma la loro maggioranza è molto risicata (hanno 219 seggi contro i 214 dei Democratici) e vari deputati ritengono come Massie che Hegseth sia inadeguato. I Democratici hanno già detto che voteranno a favore dell’ impeachment.

Se la mozione dovesse passare alla Camera dovrebbe poi essere approvata dal Senato con una maggioranza di due terzi. Anche per questo difficilmente l’ impeachment contro Hegseth funzionerà. Nella storia degli Stati Uniti soltanto due ministri sono stati messi sotto impeachment dalla Camera, e in entrambi i casi sono stati prosciolti dal Senato.

Nonostante questo, il tentativo di impeachment contro Hegseth potrebbe essere un anticipo dei prossimi due anni, in cui i Democratici avranno la maggioranza al Congresso e cercheranno di mettere alle strette l’amministrazione Trump su varie questioni. È quasi certo che, anche se non subirà l’ impeachment , Hegseth sarà chiamato a testimoniare da commissioni d’inchiesta e che il suo operato – e non soltanto il suo – subirà molti più limiti e ostacoli da parte del nuovo Congresso a maggioranza Democratica.

items.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
items.summary: Jensen Huang is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
items.content:
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.

In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.

The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.

Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.

It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.

The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.

But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.

For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.

"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.

I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.

We don't know when their affair began or ended , but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.

Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.

China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.

Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.

Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.

He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.

Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.

At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.

Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.

An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.

And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.

Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.

He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.

And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

items.title: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028
items.summary: Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the 2025 killing of the conservative activist.
items.content:
The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.

Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.

Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.

Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.

Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.

But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.

Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.

At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".

Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."

During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.

"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September.

"We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.

Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.

Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial

items.title: A Onna rinasce il forno pubblico, la prima pietra dopo il sisma del 2009
items.summary: L'edificio tornerà a disposizione del paese come luogo d'incontro
items.content:
Accanto al cantiere del forno pubblico di Onna, dove questa mattina è stata posta la prima pietra, un cartello raccoglie le fotografie della vecchia struttura. La scritta dice "La tradizione del paese torna a rivivere". Nella foto più in alto Anna Berardina Bonanni è ritratta al lavoro. Fu lei l'ultima custode dell'usanza di cuocere il pane al forno comune, praticata per decenni a Onna, frazione dell'Aquila che tutto il mondo ha conosciuto per l'altissimo numero di vittime nel terremoto del 2009.

Ex dipendente di una clinica privata, abitava lì accanto, in via della Ruetta. Morì sotto le macerie del sisma del 6 aprile, insieme ad altre 39 persone nella frazione. Alla cerimonia, all'angolo tra via del Forno e via dei Martiri, la benedizione è stata impartita da don Osman Prada. Qui ciascuno portava quel che poteva per cuocere il pane. Attorno al fuoco il paese si ritrovava. Negli ultimi anni prima del terremoto il forno era diventato anche sede della Pro loco.

"Ricostruire questo stabile significa restituire a Onna un luogo di incontro, condivisione e continuità con le proprie tradizioni", dice Angelo Palombizio, presidente del Formedil L'Aquila. Il sindaco Pierluigi Biondi ricorda che al forno "soprattutto le donne, quasi esclusivamente le donne della comunità si ritrovavano". Restituirlo all'uso pubblico, aggiunge, "significa custodirne la memoria e offrire uno spazio aperto all'incontro, alle attività culturali e alla vita quotidiana".

Per Pierluigi Frezza, presidente dell'Ance L'Aquila, il progetto mostra "come la ricostruzione riguardi i legami sociali e la qualità della vita oltre agli edifici". "Il forno di Onna tornerà a disposizione come centro sociale e di aggregazione di questa frazione", dice l'assessore all'Urbanistica Francesco De Santis. È uno degli ultimi interventi della ricostruzione del paese, dove sono ancora attivi diversi cantieri e resta aperto il nodo dei sottoservizi.

All'indomani del sisma il sistema bilaterale nazionale dell'edilizia raccolse 250 mila euro. L'iter partì nel 2009 con un protocollo tra il Comune e gli enti oggi riuniti nel Formedil L'Aquila. Il forno sarà ospitato in un edificio antisismico e ad alta efficienza energetica. I lavori sono stimati in 170 mila euro, con conclusione prevista il 1° ottobre 2027, ma c'è chi è più ottimista e si prepara a organizzare già una festa per il taglio del nastro della nuova struttura entro la fine della prossima estate.

items.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people
items.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.
items.content:
At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.

The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.

Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan originally said the death toll was 16, but the Health Minister, Kemal Memişoğlu, later announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died, taking the toll to 17.

Eyewitnesses at the scene said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.

In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.

Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued.

At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.

The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says

items.title: Russell Brand deve scontare 10 anni e mezzo di carcere per stupro
items.summary: 'Predatore sessuale protetto da fama'. Burnham promette più sostegno alle vittime
items.content:
Una pena esemplare di dieci anni e mezzo di carcere è stata inflitta all'attore britannico Russell Brand, celebrità della tv e del web nel Regno Unito e negli Usa, nonché ex marito della popstar americana Katy Perry, dopo che la settimana scorsa era stato dichiarato colpevole dello stupro di una sua fan - all'epoca dei fatti 21enne - e di molestie sessuali ai danni di altre tre donne tra il 2004 e il 2009. L'ex comico 51enne non ha mostrato alcuna emozione mentre il giudice Joel Bennathan leggeva la sentenza, sottolineando che Brand aveva agito con "sconcertante arroganza" e mostrato "disprezzo" per le sue vittime.

A pochi metri da lui la moglie Laura, con cui l'attore ha avuto tre figli, è apparsa invece sconvolta quando ha sentito il lungo periodo di detenzione deciso per il marito, anche se dopo due terzi della pena dovrebbe arrivare la libertà vigilata. "Andrà tutto bene", le ha detto Brand mentre gli agenti di custodia lo facevano uscire dall'aula della Southwark Crown Court di Londra per trasferirlo nella prigione di Wandsworth. Il giudice ha definito Brand un "predatore sessuale" protetto dalla sua fama: i reati sono avvenuti infatti quando la star della radio e della tv era all'apice del successo e si vantava di essere un playboy impietoso e provocatorio, in un'epoca in cui non c'era ancora il 'MeToo' e nel mondo dello spettacolo sembrava che tutto fosse permesso. L'attore, che si è reinventato come guru cristiano online ed è noto anche per le sue teorie complottiste, si è fatto il segno della croce stringendo un rosario fra le mani prima che una delle vittime leggesse in aula, da dietro un paravento, la sua testimonianza.

La donna ha raccontato di essere rimasta "traumatizzata" dall'aggressione subita nel 2004 in un bar di Londra. "Per molti anni, mentre la sua stella era in ascesa, era impossibile non vederlo ovunque sui media, celebrato per il suo comportamento disgustoso verso le donne come se fosse tutto uno scherzo", ha dichiarato. E la fan violentata nel 2009, dopo aver conosciuto l'ex comedian a uno dei suoi spettacoli, ha spiegato di aver temuto che "non sarebbe stata creduta" se lo avesse denunciato.

"La sua notorietà, la sua ricchezza e la sua influenza hanno creato uno squilibrio di potere che mi ha fatto sentire impotente", ha affermato, aggiungendo che la violenza ha segnato "quasi ogni aspetto" della sua vita. Sul processo, che ha profondamente colpito l'opinione pubblica britannica, è intervenuto anche il premier laburista Andy Burnham: ha reso omaggio al coraggio delle donne che si sono fatte avanti. Il primo ministro si è quindi impegnato a essere "instancabile nell'apportare tutti i miglioramenti possibili" per offrire maggiore sostegno alle vittime di violenze sessuali. Il caso ha spinto inoltre il governo a lanciare un monito al mondo dei media, accusato di non fare ancora abbastanza per proteggere le donne: "il tempo è scaduto".

Nel mirino è finita anche la Bbc, dove Brand era stato conduttore radiofonico fino al 2008. Pochi giorni fa l'emittente pubblica si era scusata per la "cultura e le carenze" di quegli anni, ma per una nota ex dipendente, la veterana dj Liz Kershaw, l'azienda aveva "permesso" il comportamento di Brand, senza intervenire quando già circolavano sospetti. E per l'attore i guai giudiziari potrebbero non essere finiti: Scotland Yard ha aperto nuove indagini per stupro dopo le denunce di altre due donne.

items.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
items.summary: Tons of chilled and frozen food was spoiled last month as fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets heated up.
items.content:
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.

Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.

The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.

Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".

He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".

France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.

The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.

Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.

Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.

In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.

If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.

On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.

Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.

The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.

Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.

In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.

The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack

UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers

If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
